author: David Delcore Staff Writer
title: Montpelier council paves the way for East State Street right-of-way resolution | Local News | timesargus.com
text:
MONTPELIER — City councilors are hoping to broker a truce in a simmering street fight that stalled a multi-million-dollar road reconstruction project at the start earlier this year. It is one that has riled residents, who insist a recently filed survey delineating the right-of-way that runs by their East State Street homes is wrong.
Questions about the right of way are not new. They were first raised by East State Street resident Jon Anderson well over a year ago, and resurfaced earlier this year when talk turned to the final design of the $8 million project.
The temperature went up earlier this month when a survey needed to leverage federal funding for a project was formally filed in the city’s land records. City councilors have since sought to turn it back down again, while protecting the city’s interest in a project, which was the subject of a successful bond vote in 2022.
Mayor Marc Gwinn took a fresh stab at that before and after the council met privately for more than an hour to consult the city’s lawyers, the surveyor, and staff.
Gwinn stressed the city is eager to work with residents on an “amicable, workable, acceptable resolution” that meets the needs of residents, while protecting the interest of the city and the broader community. That, along with rebuilding trust he feared may have been fractured in recent weeks, were priorities, the mayor said.
“One of the things that is going to be critical to this process is that we find a way to reestablish and regain and re-earn each other’s trust, particularly from us to you,” Gwinn said, lamenting the city’s objective had become muddied and misunderstood.
“Regardless of how it may have been communicated, miscommunicated, heard, misheard, the city has never had any desire to take someone’s property,” Gwinn said. “That has never been the intention.”
It still isn’t, but you would have had a hard time selling that to some residents from East State Street, and beyond, who blasted the city for a chain of events they argued rendered some affected properties impossible to sell without resolving what amounts to a cloud on their titles.
“‘Unsellable’ is a tough word to hear,” Marie Arsenlis said, before delivering a real-time history lesson that recaps the history of what is now her neighborhood going all the way back to the first survey in 1868.
Arsenlis was the first, but not the last, to question the reliability of the latest survey, even if her husband, David Ory, was more colorful in his critique.
“It makes our city look dumb,” Ory said.
According to Ory, that assessment extends to the city’s handling of the survey — one that gave it far more weight than it warranted and raised the stakes for residents.
“To publish a survey on our city’s website and then file it in our land records, that shows a right of way laid out in 1868 going through the middle of a house built in 1865 without ever publicly explaining why you think such a (right of way) is reasonable … it’s dumb,” he said, suggesting the council was at least partly responsible.
“When confronted with a dumb survey and a bad recommendation from staff to move forward with the dumb survey, the council failed to act,” he said, describing it as “both an administrative failure and a moral failure”
“You used one of the most powerful authorities given to you by our state carelessly and callously,” he said.
That wasn’t just the view from the home Ory and Arsenlis own at 74 East State St.
Patrick Coyle who bought his 89 East State St. home with no red flags, and a clean title four years ago, was livid.
“Our family is furious about this disaster of a project,” he said, adding, “This survey now claims that half our mudroom (and) possibly some of our front wall is inside this magical new right-of-way that somehow people missed for the last 160 years.”
Other East State Street residents, including Chris Owen, weighed in.
Owen first read a letter from Anderson, who he credited for flagging the right-of-way issue 15 months ago, and then waited nine months for a response from the city’s attorney.
Owen said Anderson was unable to attend the meeting and asked that he read his comments into the record.
“‘I will not sign a memorandum of understanding that limits my rights to appeal,’” Anderson wrote in the letter read by Owen. “‘We either have a final signed agreement settling the right of way, or we do not.’”
Unless a signed agreement is in place by Jan. 20, Anderson indicated he planned to appeal the survey he urged the council to “void.”
“‘I am not going to be coerced into giving up property rights the city does not need,’” Anderson wrote.
Owen said he appreciated what he perceived as “a shift in attitude” on the council’s part and was hopeful a resolution Gwinn and others on the council referenced could be reached.
“We can help the city to gain the rights to complete the East State Street project next year without overreaching into our homes’ foundations and front yards,” he said.
Getting there likely won’t involve embracing the “oops-we-made-a-mistake” suggestion offered by Dairy Lane resident Joey Crane or voiding the survey as Anderson requested. It could, councilors unanimously agreed, involve committing to narrowing the right-of-way and entering into “use agreements” with some property owners.
Gwinn and others on the council indicated they were optimistic a suitable solution could be negotiated.
“We’re committed to resolving this in a way that works for property owners,” Council Ben Doyle said.
The sentiment was echoed by other council members, including Sal Alfano, Cary Brown, and Paul Costello.
Costello assured residents they had been heard. “We get it,” he said. “We care about your neighborhood, we care about you … and we care about your rights as property owners.”
The council is also interested in keeping the long-planned full-depth reconstruction of East State Street from being delayed yet again. Votes approved a bond for the project in 2022, but historic flooding the following year prevented the city from actively pursuing it until 2025. In order to leverage funding, the U.S. Department of Agriculture has committed to the project a fresh survey had to be completed and recorded. The city has now checked that box, keeping hope that work can start next year alive.
The two-year project, which will completely reconstruct East State Street from the Main Street intersection all the way up to College Street, was initially slated to start this year.
